planting.note: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light; Lithops optica follows a strict seasonal water cycle, needing almost no water while the old pair of leaves is being reabsorbed in late winter through spring, then careful watering resuming as new leaves finish forming.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun, watering only on the strict seasonal cycle this species requires. Lithops optica is a small South African species forming a single pair of fused, plump, rounded leaves that closely mimic surrounding stones and pebbles, an extreme camouflage adaptation that gives the whole genus its common name of living stones. Each year the plant produces a new pair of leaves that draws moisture from the old pair, which shrivels and is shed, so watering during this transition period causes the plant to split or rot; water only once the old leaf pair has fully dried and new growth is established. A single white to pale lavender daisy-like flower emerges from the cleft between the leaves in fall. Give it the brightest light possible and the leanest, most mineral soil available, since overwatering and overly rich soil are by far the most common causes of failure with this species.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light; Lithops karasmontana follows a strict seasonal water cycle, needing almost no water while the old pair of leaves is being reabsorbed.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun, watering only on the strict seasonal cycle this species requires. Named for the Karas Mountains region of Namibia where it grows naturally, Lithops karasmontana forms fused, stone-like leaf pairs in shades of grey, cream, or pale pink marked with a fine network of darker channels and dots across the flattened leaf face, a camouflage pattern adapted to blend with the quartzite gravel of its native habitat. As with other lithops, each year's new leaf pair absorbs moisture from and eventually replaces the previous pair, so watering must pause during this reabsorption period to avoid splitting or rotting the plant. A white daisy-like flower emerges from the leaf cleft in fall. Give it the brightest light possible and the leanest, most mineral soil available for the healthiest, most compact growth.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light; Conophytum follows a South African winter-growing cycle, actively growing and flowering in fall through winter, then resting almost completely dry through summer.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun, following the plant's winter-growing, summer-dormant cycle. Conophytum bilobum forms small, fused, two-lobed succulent bodies, each pair of lobes resembling a tiny cleft hoof or cone, that cluster together into a dense mound over time as the plant produces new heads each season. Bright yellow to orange daisy-like flowers, often fragrant, emerge from the cleft between the lobes in fall, frequently opening only in the afternoon. Like its relative Lithops, each growing season's new body absorbs moisture from and eventually replaces the previous one, which shrivels to a papery husk that protects the new growth; withhold water almost entirely during this summer dormancy to prevent rot, resuming careful watering only as new growth becomes active in fall.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light; Split Rock is more forgiving of watering mistakes than Lithops but still needs a dry summer rest and minimal water while old leaf pairs are being reabsorbed.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, gritty succulent mix in bright light to full sun. Pleiospilos nelii, commonly called Split Rock, forms a pair (or a small cluster of pairs) of thick, rounded, greyish-brown, stone-like leaf bodies split by a shallow fissure, a mimicry adaptation similar to Lithops but on a larger, plumper scale that makes it look remarkably like a cracked pebble or small rock. Large, fragrant, bright yellow to orange daisy-like flowers, often larger than the plant body itself, appear in late summer to fall. It is somewhat more tolerant of average watering than true Lithops, but still needs a dry rest in summer and reduced water while a new leaf pair is forming and the old pair is being reabsorbed, since overwatering during this transition causes splitting or rot.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America

planting.note: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, sandy succulent mix in bright light; Fenestraria naturally grows nearly buried in sand with only the leaf tips exposed, so a shallow pot with the plant set low in gritty mix mimics its native habitat best.

directions: Grow in very well-drained, mineral, sandy succulent mix in bright light to full sun. Baby Toes forms tight clusters of small, cylindrical, upright leaves with a flattened, translucent tip that acts as a window admitting light to the leaf interior, a striking adaptation shared with a few other South African window-leaf succulents that allows the plant to grow nearly buried in sand with only these translucent tips exposed to light. Clusters slowly multiply by offsetting at the base, and yellow to white daisy-like flowers appear from the leaf tips in fall. Water sparingly, letting the mix dry completely between waterings, and reduce water further during any rest period, since this species is highly prone to rot in overly rich or constantly moist soil; a shallow pot set with the plant low in the mix best mimics its naturally sand-buried growth habit.
sources: Cactus and Succulent Society of America
